title: Earth through radar eyes
text: NISAR, a NASA–ISRO satellite, sends its own microwave pulses to Earth and listens to the echo — day and night, through clouds and smoke. The coloured strips on the globe are what it saw in the last 12 days. Green means a strong echo from inside vegetation: leaves and branches scattering the wave in every direction.

title: A forest in Spain, three days before the fire
text: Guadalajara, 14 July 2026. Yellow-green is dense vegetation; purple is open ground and fields. On 17 July a wildfire swept through these hills. NISAR passes over the same spot every 12 days, from the same angle, so we can compare like with like.

title: After the fire: the vegetation signal collapses
text: 26 July. Drag the slider to compare. Where the forest burned, the colour turns purple: 2,118 hectares lost more than half of their vegetation signal (HV fell by 3 dB or more). Unburned land next to it stays the same — so this is the fire, not a change of season or weather.

title: Three months later, no regrowth yet
text: 18 October. The chart follows one burned spot: its vegetation signal dropped from −13.5 to −21.5 dB with the fire and is still sinking (−22.2 dB), while unburned land stays near −15 dB. The dotted point in January, from another orbit, shows that summer drying did not cause the drop.

title: Another fire, a different answer
text: Muğla–Fethiye, Türkiye, burned on 28 July 2026. The scar is clear in optical images — yet the radar barely changed: only about 9 hectares lost 3 dB. Our hypothesis: NISAR's 24 cm waves mostly bounce off trunks and big branches. If the fire burned the undergrowth and the crowns but left charred trunks standing, the radar still sees a 'forest'.

title: Now it's your turn
text: Click anywhere on Earth to see what NISAR saw there, with a time machine of its past images. Press 🔥 Latest fire to jump to the newest wildfire, or 🛰 NISAR now to ride with the satellite. Click a legend item to hide a layer, and open “How we measured” for the details.
